newsitem.title: INDIA: Indians await federal budget with trepidation.
newsitem.headline: Indians await federal budget with trepidation.

text.p: Most ordinary Indians struggling to stretch their incomes to meet rising prices said on Wednesday they had become disillusioned with the country's ambitious five-year-old reform programme.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is scheduled to present the budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year (April-March) on Friday.

India's burgeoning middle class, estimated at nearly 250 million people, anxiously monitors the annual budget exercise, studying it for tax concessions but also fearful of populist measures likely to push up its cost of living.
Residents of Bombay, India's business and industrial capital, which has taken the full weight of the fall-out from reforms, said they were pessimistic about what the new budget held in store.

"This government is too weak to do anything really effective," said taxi-driver Ranjit Singh, 29. "Probably they will have to continue the reforms. But the reforms have only made things much more difficult for the common man."

Analysts predict that the budget to be presented by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's squabbling 13-party coalition will be riddled with half-measures that are compromises between factions that are bitterly divided on free markets and liberalisation.
The government's weakness is widely expected to leave most middle-class Indians, squeezed between rising inflation and slowly rising salaries, with less disposable income.
"The price of everything is rising," said housewife Sunita Pai, 34, whose husband works in middle management in a large Indian pharmaceuticals firm.

"It is difficult to manage," she added. "My husband's salary has remained virtually the same for the last five years. Every rise is taken away in income tax. I hope this time the finance minister will be able to do something."
Inflation, currently at around seven percent, hit a 58-week high of 7.99 percent in the week ended February 8, compared with 4.62 percent in the same period in 1996.
Taxi-driver Singh was particularly worried about the prospect of a fuel price hike, which many analysts say is on the cards soon after the budget.
"Already there has been one hike in the cost of fuel, and we had to revise the fares," said Singh, who estimated that he makes around 500 rupees ($14) on a good day, after expenses.
"I don't think people will accept another hike so soon. Sometimes I have to wait a whole day for a good fare."
Fuel prices were raised by an average 20 percent last July.
The Finance Ministry, in its survey of the economy released on Tuesday, hinted at the need to increase the prices of petroleum products to adjust to rising global crude oil prices.
But younger people took a brighter view.

"Liberalisation means that life has become so much more convenient now -- you can buy washing machines and televisions and gas connections without having to queue up," said 17-year-old Sheela Barjatya, a student at a Bombay university.
